content: 1. Baker et al. (2008) conducted an ecological study in New Zealand using census data from 2000 to analyze the relationship between tuberculosis (TB) cases and household crowding. The study included 1,860 census area units (CAUs) and found that TB cases were associated with crowded households, defined by a bedroom deficit of one or more. 2. Garcia-Sancho et al. examined bacteriologically confirmed TB cases in communities with fewer than 15,000 inhabitants. The study used a population-based case-control design with 42 pulmonary TB cases and 84 controls, finding a significant association between household crowding and TB. 3. Jayanthi et al. (2012) in India analyzed 300 hospital patients aged 15–75 years, of which 150 were TB-positive. The study found that households with more than four persons were more likely to have TB cases compared to those with fewer than four persons. 4. Cluver et al. (2013) in South Africa conducted a cross-sectional study involving 6,002 participants from urban and rural census sites. The study found that households with more than three persons per room were associated with pulmonary TB symptoms. 5. Corbett et al. (2009) in Zimbabwe conducted a cross-sectional study of 1,092 adults living in 46 neighborhoods. The study found that households with more than four persons per room had a higher prevalence of smear-positive TB. 6. Goldhaber-Fiebert et al. (2011) conducted a global cross-sectional study using data from 46 lowand middle-income countries. The study found that an additional person per room increased the likelihood of TB symptoms. 7. Gyawali et al. (2012) in Nepal studied 802 household contacts of 184 pulmonary TB index cases. The study found that households with two to three persons per room had a higher prevalence of culture-confirmed pulmonary TB compared to those with fewer than two persons per room. 8. Harling et al. (2013) in Brazil used a retrospective cohort design to analyze 719,663 notified TB cases. The study found that households with more than two persons per sleeping room were associated with higher rates of pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB. 9. Hill et al. (2006) in Gambia conducted a case-control study of 100 TB cases and 200 controls. The study found that households with at least four persons and at least two persons per room had a higher prevalence of sputum culture-positive pulmonary TB. 10. Lakshmi et al. (2012) in India studied 126 women with TB and 252 controls. The study found that households with four or more persons per room were associated with sputum culture-positive pulmonary TB. 11. Lienhardt et al. (2005) conducted a case-control study in Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, and Gambia involving 2,376 participants. The study found that household crowding, defined as persons per room, was associated with sputum culture-positive pulmonary TB. 12. Larcombe et al. studied 129 households and found that self-reported TB cases were associated with higher numbers of persons per room. 13. Tipayamongkholgul et al. (2005) in Thailand conducted a case-control study of 130 TB cases and 130 controls. The study found that households with five or more persons per room were associated with hospital-diagnosed TB. 14. Tornée et al. (2004) in Thailand studied 500 household contacts of sputum-smear-positive pulmonary TB patients. The study found that households with three or more persons per room had a higher prevalence of positive tuberculin skin tests. 15. Soborg et al. conducted a cross-sectional study involving 1,797 participants. The study used interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) and tuberculin skin tests (TST) to assess TB infection in relation to household crowding. 16. Wanyeki et al. found that an increase in persons per room was associated with a higher likelihood of active TB diagnosis in a case-control study involving 545 cases and 5,450 controls. 17. Irfan et al. (2017) in Bangladesh conducted a case-control study of 178 TB cases and 179 controls. The study found that households with two or more persons per room were associated with TB. 18. Kapoor et al. (2016) in India analyzed abstract data from 893 TB cases and 333 controls. The study found that households with three to five persons per room were associated with TB. 19. Khan et al. (2016) in Canada conducted a case-control study of 44 Inuit TB cases and 156 controls. The study found that households with more than one person per room were associated with TB. 20. Pelissari et al. (2017) in Brazil conducted an ecological study of 63,907 TB cases in 3,839 municipalities. The study found that a higher proportion of the population living in crowded households was associated with TB. 21. Tesema et al. (2015) in Ethiopia conducted a case-control study of 218 TB cases and 437 controls. The study found that households with less than 4 m² per person per room were associated with TB. 22. Islam et al. (2013) in India conducted a cross-sectional study of children under five years of age. The study found that household crowding was associated with a higher prevalence of acute respiratory infections. 23. Al Jarousha et al. (2014) in the West Bank and Gaza Strip conducted a cross-sectional study of 1,853 children hospitalized for acute bacterial meningitis. The study found that households with more than three persons per room were associated with bacterial meningitis. 24. Rao et al. (2010) in Guatemala conducted a cross-sectional survey of 701 individuals in 184 households. The study found that household crowding was associated with water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) risk factors. 25. De Wals et al. (2005) in Canada conducted a case-control study of 74 individuals with confirmed serogroup C meningococcal disease. The study found that household crowding was associated with the effectiveness of the serogroup C meningococcal polysaccharide vaccine. 26. Matthew et al. (2014) in India conducted a cross-sectional study of 2,333 children with pneumonia. The study found that household overcrowding was associated with bacterial etiology of childhood community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). 27. Grant et al. (2012) in New Zealand conducted a case-control study of 428 children hospitalized with pneumonia and 351 controls. The study found that households with more than one person per room were associated with pneumonia. 28. Okello et al. (2012) in Uganda conducted a case-control study of 243 cases and 243 controls. The study found that households with more than eight people were associated with rheumatic heart disease. 29. Prietsch et al. (2008) in Brazil conducted a cross-sectional study of 775 children aged 0–59 months. The study found that households with more than four people per room were associated with acute lower respiratory illness. 30. Reisman et al. (2013) in Alaska conducted a cross-sectional study of 12,535 individuals. The study found that household crowding was associated with pneumococcal colonization. 31. Deutch et al. (2004) in Denmark conducted a case-control study of 1,222 cases and 24,549 controls. The study found that household crowding, defined by square meters per person, was associated with meningococcal disease. 32. Kristensen et al. (2006) in South Africa conducted a prospective cohort study of 571 children aged 0–1 years. The study found that the number of adults and siblings sharing a bedroom with the child was associated with acute respiratory infections. 33. Cardoso et al. (2004) in Brazil conducted a case-control study of 396 cases and 336 controls. The study found that the number of people sleeping in a child’s bedroom was associated with acute lower respiratory disease. 34. Jain et al. (2011) in New Zealand conducted a retrospective cohort study of 1,249 individuals. The study found that the proportion of crowded households in census area units was associated with acute rheumatic fever. 35. Alemayehu et al. (2017) in Ethiopia conducted a cross-sectional study of 240 healthy children and adolescents. The study found that household crowding was associated with nasal carriage of meningococcal isolates. 36. Alvarado-Esquivel et al. conducted a case-control study of 125 miners and 250 controls. The study found that household crowding was associated with Toxoplasma gondii infection. 37. Auguet et al. (2016) in the United Kingdom conducted an ecological study. The study found that overcrowding, based on bedroom occupancy rating, was associated with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). 38. Brander et al. (2017) in Kenya conducted a cross-sectional study of 292 children presenting with acute diarrhea. The study found that household crowding was associated with multi-drug-resistant enteric infections. 39. Bruden et al. found that household crowding was associated with respiratory syncytial virus in an ecological study of 1,903 children. 40. Chandrasekhar et al. found that household crowding was associated with influenza in an ecological study of 33,515 laboratory-confirmed influenza-associated hospitalizations. 41. Chattopadhyay et al. (2016) in India conducted a cross-sectional study of 258 coal-based sponge iron plant workers. The study found that household crowding was associated with respiratory disease. 42. Da Fonseca Lima et al. (2016) in Brazil conducted a case-control study of 407 pneumonia cases and 407 controls. The study found that households with two or more persons sleeping in the same room as the child were associated with pneumonia. 43. Diaz et al. (2015) in Mexico conducted a case-control study of children under five years of age. The study found that households with three or more persons per bedroom were associated with acute respiratory infections. This detailed summary preserves the specificity of the original data while presenting it in a clear and professional manner.
